entries.milestone: Receipt channel coverage bounded, and a spending recommendation corrected
entries.finding: GDELT DOC ArticleList returns HTTP 429 to a residential IP at 16-second spacing -- more than three times its own stated 'one every 5 seconds' limit. The throttle is therefore NOT purely IP reputation and not purely interval; the refusal text points at query size ('for larger queries') and directs high-traffic users to the bulk n-gram files.
entries.measurement: Direct per-query probe, 16s apart: pakistan_west q1 (222 chars) 429, q2 (146 chars) HTTP 200 with 10 articles, gulf_energy q1 (213 chars) 429, q2 (20 chars) 429. The lane's own run scored 3 of 5 channels twice in a row with the identical split, so this is stable rather than transient.
entries.mechanism: A channel is marked unavailable if ANY of its queries fails. The five channels need 1,1,1,2,2 queries under the signed 230-character partition rule, and the two that need two queries are exactly the two that fail -- twice the exposure per channel. pakistan_west runs FIRST, so this is not late-run exhaustion.
entries.correction: I previously told the founder a VPS would fix the throttled receipt channels, citing the events backfill that succeeded from this machine. That inference was too strong. The events FILE endpoint is not throttled and a clean IP fixes it; the DOC API throttles this machine too. A VPS should still help receipts, because a dedicated IP is not shared with thousands of CI jobs, but it is not the answer for this lane and must not be bought on that promise. The events-backfill justification for the VPS is unaffected and remains measured.
entries.why_not_fixed_here: Every lever is signature-bound. maximum_requests_per_run (7), request_interval_seconds (15) and the 230-character query partition rule all live in governance/gdelt_receipt_identity_profile.json, which the founder's 2026-08-15 activation signature covers. Widening the interval, splitting fewer queries, or reordering channels all change the signed profile and need a re-activation ceremony. Nothing here was forced.
options_for_the_ceremony: Raise request_interval_seconds so a run paces well under the observed refusal rate, accepting a longer lane.
Raise the query partition ceiling so no channel needs two requests, which removes the doubled exposure entirely.
Move the lane to the bulk n-gram files, which is what GDELT's own refusal text recommends for high-traffic users.
Leave it, and publish 3 of 5 channels with the other two honestly unavailable -- which is what happens today and is not a failure.
entries.non_double_counting: A measured limit on a source is diagnosis, not evidence for any scoring domain.
blockers: Every remedy changes a signature-bound profile.
entries.next_safe_action: Present the four options as a decision packet; change nothing until the founder picks one.

But src/evidence_outputs.py is a separate, real, template-driven engine that compiles a board-brief draft alongside the other three products, and its docstring states the property that matters: all prose comes from fixed templates over registered fields, and no model writes facts, numbers, dates, citations, confidence, causation, forecasts or recommendations. That is one founder ceremony, and it unblocks the largest scoring domain in the plan.
entries.three_corrections_note: This entry has now been corrected twice, both times in the same direction and for the same reason: I read a description and reported it as the state of the world. The docstring understated the offline bundle; conflating two module names understated the brief. Both were caught only by running the code. The rule this keeps teaching: for any claim about what exists, execute it -- a description is evidence about intent, never about bytes.

entries.milestone: The dependency between the three biggest domains established
entries.correction: One message earlier I told the founder that enrolling a release signer unblocks the 12-point proof-product domain: enrol, sign a release, run the compiler. The middle step does not exist. The only thing in the repository that builds a signed canonical release is src/oges_fixture.py, whose own docstring states its private keys are public test vectors that must never appear in a production trust registry. There is no production release builder.
entries.what_a_release_actually_requires: schemas/canonical-release.schema.json requires an objects array of {object_type, object_id, path, file_sha256, record_sha256} where object_type is one of evidence_item, entity, event, exposure_edge or universe_release, plus per-type counts, plus digests of the schema, method, rights, rights-signer and release-signer registries, plus a rights snapshot, plus the signature. In other words a release is a manifest OVER a bitemporal evidence graph of real India entities, events, evidence items and exposure edges.
entries.the_actual_structure: The three largest domains are not parallel. They are one chain: the evidence and rights kernel (9 points) produces canonical objects; the India vertical (8 points) is the universe of entities, events and exposure edges those objects describe; a canonical release is the signed manifest over them; and the four proof products (12 points) are what the EXISTING compiler emits from that release. 29 of 46 points run through one sequence, and its last stage is already built.
entries.why_this_is_good_news_anyway: The end of the chain is done and template-locked. src/evidence_outputs.py needs no model, invents no facts, and is waiting on input rather than on authorship. Nobody has to design the products; the work is upstream, where it was always going to be, and it is now known to be upstream rather than assumed to be four separate builds.
entries.what_changes_in_planning: Do not schedule the proof products as an independent tranche and do not promise them from a ceremony. Schedule the evidence kernel and the India vertical, and treat the release plus the compiler run as the short step that follows. The release-signer enrolment ceremony is still needed and still correct -- it is simply not sufficient on its own.
entries.authority_required: founder_enrolment_ceremony_eventually; no authority blocks the upstream build
entries.non_double_counting: Establishing a dependency is diagnosis. The 29 points along this chain are claimable once each stage exists and is accepted, each in its own domain and never twice.
entries.next_safe_action: Build the canonical-object emitters for real IGRM evidence, starting with the object types the India vertical needs, rather than anything further downstream.

entries.milestone: Build order for the canonical graph established by walking it, not by planning it
entries.method: Tried to emit ONE real canonical object -- India as an entity -- and let the schema refuse until it was right. Three refusals in sequence, each informative: schema_version must be 1.0.0 not 0.1.0; an identifier needs effective_start and effective_end; and an identifier needs evidence_ids, which common.schema.json defines as a NON-EMPTY id array.
entries.the_finding: You cannot assert that India's ISO 3166 code is IND without citing an evidence item that supports it. The schema refuses the entity outright. The same rule runs through the graph: event requires evidence_links, exposure_edge requires evidence_ids, and evidence_item itself requires 30 fields including rights_use, rights_decision_id, privacy_class, content_availability, artifact_sha256 and verification_status.
entries.why_this_matters: The build order is not a planning choice, it is enforced. Evidence items come first; entities, events and exposure edges may only exist by citing them; and a canonical release is the signed manifest over the result. An attempt to seed a universe of India entities first -- which is the intuitive way to start, and the way I was about to start -- would have been refused at the first identifier. The schema is doing exactly what the whole project claims to do: it will not let an assertion exist without its evidence.
entries.what_was_verified: canonical_objects.seal_record produces a stable record_sha256 for a well-formed record and the seal changes on a one-character edit. The sealing primitives work; what is missing is the emitters that produce real records to seal.
next_build_order: evidence_item emitters over sources IGRM already holds rights for, since every other object type must cite them
entity emitters whose identifiers cite those evidence items
event and exposure_edge emitters, which are the India vertical proper
the canonical release manifest over all of it, then the enrolment ceremony and the existing compiler
entries.non_double_counting: Establishing a build order is diagnosis, not evidence.
entries.next_safe_action: Write the evidence_item emitter for one rights-cleared source and seal one real evidence record.

entries.milestone: Canonical chain advanced two stages; the third refused with a stated reason
entries.built: evidence_item and entity emitters, both real, both schema-valid, both sealed, 19 hostile tests. 15 evidence records from the published receipt identity and 15 provisional publisher entities whose identifiers cite them.
entries.why_events_stop_here: event requires a coding block of rule_id, rule_version, implementation_sha256, status, coder_ids, adjudicator_ids and limitation_codes, and an event_class from a closed enum -- armed_conflict, diplomatic_action, trade_restriction and so on. No registered rule in this repository classifies a headline into that enum; the only adjacent contract, source_frame_entity_foundry.json, is rights_blocked_contract_only. Emitting events anyway would mean inventing a classification and stamping it with a coding block that names no real rule, which is precisely what that block exists to prevent.
entries.the_deeper_reason: A news article evidences that something was REPORTED, not that it happened. The schema already provides the honest vocabulary for that -- record_status candidate, publication_phase provisional, and an evidence_link role of allegation -- so the shape is expressible. What is missing is not vocabulary but authority: somebody has to register the rule that maps a headline to a class, version it, and pin its implementation digest. That is a methodology decision, and methodology decisions are exactly what the independent methods reviewer exists to attack.
entries.what_this_is_not: This is not a blocker in the sense of something broken. Two of five stages are built and the schema accepted them. The chain simply reaches a point where the next artifact requires a registered rule rather than more code, and writing the code first would produce a graph full of confident classifications nobody can defend.
entries.next_safe_action: Register a coding rule for the receipt channels as a machine_candidate with explicit limitation_codes, or decide events come from a source that already carries classification (GDELT events, which IGRM already ingests as counts) rather than from headlines. Both are methodology choices and both should be visible to the methods reviewer.
entries.non_double_counting: Two emitters existing is build progress, not accepted evidence.
blockers: No registered coding rule maps a headline to an event_class.

entries.milestone: The real precondition for the four proof products, verified in code
entries.correction: I told the founder twice that four real proof products were one enrolment and one signature away. That is wrong. src/evidence_outputs.py refuses with output_event_not_in_release unless the event_id it is given exists in the release, and it then projects exposure FROM that event TO a target entity. The compiler is event-centric: a product set is compiled about a specific event, not about a graph in general. Our release contains zero events, so signing it would produce nothing.
entries.what_i_got_right_and_wrong: Two separate claims got tangled. A canonical RELEASE genuinely does not need events -- the schema sets every per-type count minimum to zero and our unsigned release validates but for the signature. That part of the correction stands. The four PRODUCTS do need an event, which was my original position before I overturned it. Both halves were half right, and only reading the compiler settled it.
entries.the_true_precondition: Four proof products require, in order: a registered coding rule that maps something to an event_class; events emitted under it; exposure edges from those events to target entities; then the release, the enrolment and the signature. The coding rule is a methodology decision, so the binding constraint on the largest scoring domain is a decision, not a ceremony and not engineering.
entries.what_the_current_release_is_still_good_f: It is a real, sealed, schema-conformant canonical release lacking only a signature, over 15 evidence items, 15 entities and a universe that states its own denominator and its dark channels. It is exactly the artifact an independent reviewer can be handed to check the evidence and rights chain end to end, and it is the thing the enrolment ceremony exists to sign. It simply is not yet an input the product compiler will accept.
entries.founder_impact: Do not spend a signature expecting products. The enrolment ceremony is still worth doing when convenient, because it unblocks the release and the offline bundle, but the products wait on the event coding decision.
blockers: The product compiler refuses a release with no events.
entries.next_safe_action: Put the event-coding choice to the methods reviewer as the first question, since it gates 12 points and is exactly the kind of decision an independent methodologist should make rather than an implementer.

entries.milestone: The daily lane's 15 wasted minutes explained by arithmetic rather than guessed at
entries.observation: Daily run 31965802847 logged: the action 'Chokepoint salience tail + divergence JSON (V2-4, ~4 requests)' has timed out after 15 minutes. It is continue-on-error, so it did NOT fail the run -- the run failed on a gate syntax error I introduced separately. What it does is burn a quarter hour and refresh nothing, leaving chokepoints.json among the stale payloads.
entries.the_arithmetic: src/fetch_gdelt.py sets TIMEOUT_S=420 (7 minutes per request, deliberately generous because a multi-year timelinevol query takes GDELT minutes to compute and a read timeout means accepted-and-working), SLEEP_S=15 between requests, and RETRIES=6. The step fetches about 4 channels. Floor if each channel times out once: 4*(420+15) = 1740s = 29.0 minutes. Two slow channels alone are 14.5 minutes. Worst case with the retry budget on a single channel: 43.5 minutes. The step cap is 15.
entries.diagnosis: The cap is smaller than the module's own worst case by roughly a factor of two, so the step cannot complete on any day GDELT is slow. This is not a mystery failure; it is a cap that was never derived from the bounds of the code it caps -- the same defect morning.yml documents having made three times before someone wrote the arithmetic down.
entries.why_i_did_not_just_raise_it: morning.yml's own comment says it: the right fix is a cheaper gate, not a bigger cap, and the third raise 'should be the last one that works by arithmetic rather than by fixing the cause'. Raising this to 30 minutes lengthens a lane that already runs an hour, to protect a comparison payload that never enters the composite. The options are a real trade and should be chosen with the numbers visible, not by an agent picking one at 2am.
options: Raise the step cap to 30 minutes and accept a longer daily lane.
Pass a reduced per-request timeout for this lane only, since a 14-day tail merge does not need the 7-minute ceiling that a 3,447-day backfill does.
Give the module a wall-clock deadline it respects internally, so it returns partial-and-honest instead of being killed mid-request.
Leave it. The step is continue-on-error, the payload never enters the composite, and 15 minutes of a nightly lane is a cheap price for not touching a working publish path.
entries.authority_required: none_technically; a decision about lane duration
entries.next_safe_action: Choose an option with the arithmetic in view. Option 3 is the only one that fixes the cause rather than the symptom.

entries.milestone: Audit finding corrected: right conclusion, fabricated derivation
entries.the_error: I audited every timed network step against 'its module's worst case' and reported that daily.yml runs src.fetch_events under a 15-minute cap against a ~36-minute worst case. That number came from fetch_gdelt's constants -- TIMEOUT_S 420, SLEEP_S 15 -- and src/fetch_events.py does not import fetch_gdelt at all. It uses urllib against GDELT's static events FILE endpoint, which is a different service with different limits. I applied one module's numbers to another module and published the result in a commit message.
entries.recomputed_from_the_real_constants: fetch_events sets TIMEOUT_S=120, RETRIES=3, SLEEP_S=1.0 (commented 'static CDN files, not the rate-limited API'), with backoff 5/10/15s between attempts. daily.yml runs --update 5. Worst case: 5 * (3*120 + 30 + 1) = 1955s = 32.6 minutes against a 15-minute cap.
entries.so_the_conclusion_survives: The cap is still smaller than the worst case, by roughly a factor of two, and fetch_events still has no deadline. But I reached that conclusion by accident: the fabricated figure happened to land near the real magnitude. A number that is right for the wrong reason is not evidence, and the audit script that produced it hardcoded a WORST table mapping modules to constants they do not all use.
entries.the_typical_case_matters_too: Measured tonight rather than modelled: eight days backfilled in about two minutes from this machine. So the 32.6-minute figure is a genuine ceiling and a rare one -- it bites only when GDELT's file CDN is slow or erroring, which is exactly when a lane most needs to fail legibly rather than be killed.
entries.what_i_did_not_do: Add the deadline to fetch_events. It is a different fetch path from the two modules I have just worked in, so the mechanism would need reading rather than copying, and I have made the act-before-reading error enough times in one session that starting a third data-path change on a freshly-green publish path is the wrong call. Recorded with the corrected arithmetic so the next session starts from a true number.
entries.non_double_counting: Diagnosis, and a correction to a previous diagnosis.
entries.next_safe_action: Give fetch_events a deadline modelled on its own urllib path, not copied from fetch_gdelt's.

entries.milestone: ci.yml extraction locked on executability, not just completeness
entries.how_it_was_found: Reading the log of daily run 31965802847, which failed like the six before it. The last error in the chain was 'publish refused: the committed CI gate is red on 1775e682. Failing check: |. Detail: scripts/gate.sh: eval: line 217: syntax error near unexpected token |'. That is my own bug from earlier the same day: I added emitter checks to ci.yml as `run: |` blocks, and gate.sh extracts `^[[:space:]]+run: ` and evals each extracted line, so it evaled a bare pipe. Current main is clean -- the fix landed -- but nothing stopped it recurring.
entries.why_the_existing_test_could_not_catch_it: tests/test_gate_matches_ci.py::test_the_gate_picks_up_every_ci_command compares `gate.sh --print` against a Python regex re-derivation of the same ci.yml. For `run: |` BOTH capture the bare `|` by the same rule, agree, and pass. The file whose stated thesis is 'a check that cannot fail the way the real one does' contained one. Completeness was locked; executability was not.
entries.the_lock: Two tests, because one does not cover the class. `bash -n` on each extracted line catches `|`, `|-`, `>` and anything else that is not valid shell. An explicit block-scalar check catches `>-`, which bash -n PASSES -- it is a redirect creating a file named `-`, exit 0 -- so a `run: >-` step would eval clean and the gate would report that check GREEN having executed nothing. The silent variant is the dangerous one.
entries.not_hypothetical: .github/workflows/canonical-graph.yml uses `run: >-` today, so the idiom is already in the author's hands; only ci.yml is read by gate.sh, which is why this is a lock rather than an incident.
entries.verification: Mutation-tested against ci.yml, restoring from backup between runs. `run: |` fails both new tests; `run: >-` fails only the marker test; the pre-existing completeness test stays GREEN in both cases, which is the finding. Clean tree: 7 passed. ruff exit 0, mypy exit 0 over 144 files. Exit codes read unpiped.
entries.self_assessment: This closes a hole I opened. It earns no points: it is repair of my own defect plus the missing lock, not new evidence.

entries.milestone: morning.yml stamps before it writes; nine payloads ship unattributed
entries.how_it_was_found: Chasing my own regression. 492bbaa had overwritten docs/data/chokepoints.json with a one-stage build that dropped _meta.citation, _meta.codebook and _meta.source; the measurements were byte-identical, only the attribution was gone. Asking what SHOULD have caught that led to stamp_meta.audit(), which reports nine payloads on main with none of license, citation, codebook or source.
entries.the_structural_finding: test_stamp_meta_runs_after_every_payload_writer reads WORKFLOWS/'daily.yml' by name, so the invariant has never been evaluated for any other lane. Run against daily.yml the after-stamp set is empty. Run against morning.yml it is nine: blind_spot, episode_actors, event_ledger, evolution_engine, exposure, monthly, predictability, publish_shares, world_state. morning.yml stamps at step 6 of 24 and its Derived lanes block rewrites payloads afterwards. morning.yml is the lane that publishes the 06:00 contract, so the unstamped payloads are the ones that ship.
entries.why_no_gate_caught_it: The check that would catch it, test_the_live_site_keeps_the_codebook_promise, exists and is correct, but is marked @pytest.mark.live. Both the publish gate and daily.yml step 6 run pytest with -m 'not live'. The marker's documented purpose is to exclude assertions that can go spuriously red when a weekly lane runs a day late; this assertion reads docs/data/*.json off disk with no clock and no network, so it can never be spuriously red, and it is excluded anyway.
entries.what_was_done: A ratchet, not the fix: the after-stamp set may shrink, never grow, and a second test fails once it empties so the ratchet is removed deliberately. Mutation-tested both directions.
entries.what_was_deliberately_not_done: The repair is a reorder of the 06:00 contract lane. assistant_answers records a source_sha256 of the payloads it cites and must follow the last rewrite, while world_state, event_ledger, evolution_engine and product_catalog currently run after IT. morning.yml cannot be rehearsed end to end locally and a wrong reorder means no publish at 06:00. Left for the founder rather than attempted unattended at 04:30.
entries.my_own_error_inside_the_fix: The first MORNING_UNSTAMPED was built from a hand-rolled 'writes a payload' regex rather than the module's own WRITES_PAYLOAD, and got the membership wrong in both directions -- listed provenance, missed world_state. Caught by the test failing on a clean tree. Same re-derivation error as the gate lock two commits earlier, made while writing the fix for it.
entries.self_assessment: No points. One repair of my own regression, one ratchet, one defect handed over unfixed and named.

entries.milestone: Root cause of the stale derived plane: two lanes, one publish cursor
entries.the_symptom_the_founder_reported: Stale article sources and stale payloads, alongside a site that was itself current. Both halves were true at once, which is why it went five days without diagnosis.
entries.the_mechanism: morning.yml publishes the 06:00 contract; daily.yml refreshes the derived plane. daily.yml's Run pipeline step asked src.run_daily to publish D-1 unconditionally. require_ordered_target demands the exact next UNPUBLISHED day before UTC D0. So on every day the contract lane SUCCEEDED, daily.yml found nothing to publish and raised final_target_invalid. GitHub then skipped every step after it.
entries.measured: Run 31975757637: 20 steps succeeded, 1 failed, 27 skipped. The skipped set includes step 23 Derived lanes, step 26 Freshness audit, step 40 Stamp universal _meta on every payload, and step 42 Machine answers. The commit step logged 'refusing every derived docs change' and banked raw evidence only. Every scheduled daily-update run has concluded failure since 2026-08-12; morning.yml's 01:12 UTC schedule on 08-16 succeeded.
entries.why_it_stayed_hidden: The product looked right. igrm.in served 2026-08-15 finalized throughout, because the contract lane was green. A chronically red lane beside a healthy public artifact reads as a nuisance rather than as the reason a whole plane stopped refreshing.
entries.the_pattern: Fourth occurrence in this repo of a gate asserting the world is already good and thereby blocking the work that keeps it good. The three earlier ones are recorded at the publisher, the receipt predecessor and the derived-data plane. This is the cross-lane variant: two lanes share one 'next unpublished day' cursor, whichever runs first consumes it, and the second fails by design.
entries.the_fix: Ask --next-target, an already-supported flag, and treat 'none' as skip-and-continue rather than an error. --target is now the value require_ordered_target actually demands rather than a blind D-1: identical when they agree, and when they differ D-1 could only ever have failed, so a backlog now walks forward one ordered day at a time instead of wedging.
entries.verification: Locked behaviourally, not by text match: the test extracts the real step body from the workflow, substitutes what GitHub substitutes, and executes it against a stubbed python. Mutation-tested with one-token changes -- `if false` (pre-fix, never skip) fails exactly the regression test; `if true` (always skip) fails exactly the two publish tests. ruff 0, mypy 0, 56 passed. A first attempt at the removal mutant mangled the YAML and was discarded rather than counted, caught by the suite's own shell-validity test.
entries.unverified_at_time_of_writing: A dispatched run on this commit is in flight to confirm the 27 steps now execute and the job goes green. The claim that the fix works is not yet earned.
entries.self_assessment: No points. This is the diagnosis the founder asked for on the first message of the session, arrived at after three of my own defects were cleared out of the way first.

entries.milestone: GDELT attribution restored; two classes of switched-off check found
entries.the_breach: GDELT grants unlimited use on one condition: any use or redistribution must cite The GDELT Project and link https://www.gdeltproject.org/. Measured: docs/codebook.html named GDELT 27 times and linked it 0 times; codebook.md 27/0; methodology.html 14/0; of 17 GDELT-derived published payloads, 2 carried the link. Thirteen public pages named the source without crediting it while asserting CC BY 4.0 over the derived output. A public index built primarily on GDELT was failing its supplier's only requirement, on the pages a reviewer opens first.
entries.how_found: The adversarial half of a rights-decision review, which was looking for OVERclaiming and instead surfaced a live condition failure on shipped artifacts. Verified independently before acting.
entries.fixed: At the shared-footer layer in src/site_shell.py so all 40 shell routes inherit it, plus index.html (not a shell route), corrections.md and datasheet.md (markdown the shell does not reach). The codebook quotes the condition verbatim rather than paraphrasing, so a reader inheriting the data can see it binds them too. Locked by tests/test_upstream_attribution.py: any public page naming GDELT must link it, 44 assertions.
entries.conflict_resolved_in_favour_of_the_licen: test_vintages_page asserted that page carries NO external origin. vintages.html names GDELT twice so the condition binds it. A licence obligation outranks a self-imposed layout rule; the accommodation is one exact URL rather than a relaxation to 'any external origin', so the rule still forbids third-party content and links to unaudited claims.
entries.second_finding_switched_off_checks: Swept for tests carrying @pytest.mark.live whose bodies make no network call: thirteen exist. Every gate runs pytest with -m 'not live'. Running the whole live set, exactly ONE fails -- the genuinely time-varying staleness assertion. The other twelve are time-invariant checks excluded from every gate for no reason. tests/test_published_data_sanity.py is the sharpest case: its docstring says it exists because wiki_hindi.json shipped bare NaN for an hour on 2026-08-07, and being marked live it could not prevent the exact defect it was written for. Its six assertions now gate. The remaining seven were left alone deliberately -- changing what gates a publish is not a bulk sweep to do at 04:00.
entries.third_finding_security_plane_caught_me: lane-health.yml as first written asked for issues: write. src/security_integrity.py refuses any workflow whose permission scopes fall outside {contents, actions} and rejected it. Widening a registered security scope is a founder decision, so the lane was redesigned to fit the policy -- contents: read only, escalation via run status and a job summary -- rather than the policy relaxed to fit the lane.
entries.rights_drafts: 15 sources drafted and adversarially attacked: 10 SAFE, 2 UNDERCLAIMS, 2 UNVERIFIABLE, 1 OVERCLAIMS. The attack pass caught india_ogd_port_trade_2019_20 claiming publish_extract its terms do not grant, and caught both GDELT drafts being too NARROW -- signing as drafted would have left event_ledger.json permanently blocked while recording a completed review. imf_portwatch and cow_mids are terms_unavailable and grant nothing rather than a guess.
entries.self_assessment: No points. One live compliance breach closed, two classes of check restored to gating, one security control respected rather than widened. All repair and hardening, no new evidence.

hostile_review_findings.title: Refusal artifact accepted a backdated evaluation stamp under the signed rights registry
hostile_review_findings.mechanism: event_ledger.verify_payload_bytes derives the evaluation instant from the payload's own _meta.generated, then recomputes build(evaluated_at=that) and byte-compares. Under the founder's signed 2026-08-15 registry, _meta.generated is the ONLY field that varies with evaluated_at (measured by building at two instants and diffing every leaf), so a backdated stamp reproduces itself byte-for-byte and the comparison cannot see it.
hostile_review_findings.bounded_severity: Forward-dating was always refused (refusal_evaluation_time_future). No field other than _meta.generated can be forged; the byte comparison still covers them. The open window was backdating from contract_effective to now -- four days on 2026-08-16, widening each day the contract-effective date recedes. It is a freshness lie in a value-free refusal artifact, not arbitrary content forgery.
hostile_review_findings.why_the_checkpoint_missed_it: It PASSES at 2f4d4264. The checkpoint's own rights state left another field varying with evaluation time, so the recomputation caught the tamper. The weakness appears only once real signatures land -- the configuration that actually ships. Neither H0's tests nor CI would have caught it.
hostile_review_findings.remediation: verify_payload_bytes now bounds the evaluation stamp by the already-registered MAX_REFUSAL_RELEASE_AGE when release_instant is None; the release path already enforced the same bound through release_instant.
hostile_review_findings.deadlock_check: Both callers verify the current artifact, never a historical one, and --verify-payload is wired into no workflow (CI runs only --check). A freshness bound on a historical verifier would have rebuilt the transition-deadlock pattern; it does not here.
hostile_review_findings.regression_tests: tests/test_event_ledger_backdating.py -- 6 tests pinning both edges plus the mechanism itself. Proven to bite: fix stashed, 2 fail; restored, 6 pass.

hostile_review_findings.title: H0 requires a public schema copy that exists in no commit of the lineage
hostile_review_findings.mechanism: src/endpoint_unavailable.py declares DOCS_SCHEMA_RELATIVE = docs/schemas/endpoint-unavailable.schema.json and the publish path requires it to exist and be byte-identical to the root schemas/ copy, refusing endpoint_unavailable_schema_bytes_mismatch otherwise. The checkpoint shipped the root copy and the code demanding both, but never the docs copy.
hostile_review_findings.evidence: The same tests fail identically at 2f4d4264 on its own parent 4c4eec49. The path is absent at 4c4eec49, 2f4d4264, c363af12 and eb050bd5.
hostile_review_findings.remediation: Added byte-identical; sha256 18da4675a4e68c93418b94384616c2bdaec2712b91c1a1935fb5a570042775d6 matches the code's PINNED_SCHEMA_SHA256.

hostile_review_findings.title: The publisher's decision-signature pin does not know the founder's 2026-08-15 decisions
hostile_review_findings.mechanism: src/endpoint_unavailable.py iterates every approved registry row and requires each row's signature digest in PINNED_DECISION_SIGNATURE_SHA256, which holds exactly one entry (the ngrams aggregate decision). The two rows approved on 2026-08-15 -- gdelt_doc_api and gdelt_bq_webngrams -- have no pin, so publish_final_cas.sh refuses with endpoint_unavailable_decision_signature_invalid.
hostile_review_findings.signature_verification_performed: All three approved decisions were verified as 64-byte Ed25519 signatures over the exact committed artifact bytes under the enrolled, unrevoked human:igrm-ngram-rights-reviewer key, with each artifact digest matching its registry row. All three VALID.
hostile_review_findings.why_claude_did_not_complete_it: Registering the two pins requires coordinated edits across five anchors: the constant in src/endpoint_unavailable.py, PUBLIC_TREE_HELPER_SHA256 in src/security_integrity.py, the security registry entry, and a hard-coded git blob OID (aa00529c74592a3001ce87157bfb6105a59ac595) embedded twice in each of scripts/publish_final_cas.sh and scripts/ship.sh -- both themselves sha-pinned publisher scripts. That multi-anchor design exists so no single automated actor can quietly widen what the publisher trusts. A trial edit was made, verified to move the refusal forward one layer, and then REVERTED so no half-registered state was frozen; src/endpoint_unavailable.py is back at its exact H0 bytes (digest 442cb0ad).

founder_decision_packets.exact_question: Push the two local commits that repair the 06:00 IST contract and thicken the receipts cadence?
founder_decision_packets.recommended_option: Push. The audit fix is the sole reason the 2026-08-15 final refused, and every further morning will refuse the same way until it lands.
founder_decision_packets.alternatives: Hold for an independent reviewer. Cost: one missed contract per day held, and the 42 stale payloads keep CI red.
founder_decision_packets.consequences: After the push, the next cron shot or the watchdog publishes the exact D-1 final; the enrichment lanes then refresh the stale payloads and CI's only red clears on its own.
founder_decision_packets.what_continues_without_a_response: All H0, evidence-plane, and India-vertical engineering continues; only the live contract stays broken.
